traits: Carrot-shaped, silvery, wiggles side to side as it runs
Three long tail bristles at the rear
Found in books, boxes, and closets — anywhere starchy and still

look_alikes.difference: Silverfish are silvery and prefer humid spots like bathrooms; firebrats are mottled gray-brown and prefer hot, dry spots like near water heaters and furnaces.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the body color and where it was found (humid vs. hot/dry area).

copy.what_it_means: Silverfish are older than dinosaurs and mostly a storage-box nuisance — they feed on paper, glue, and starchy materials. Lots of them signals a humidity problem worth fixing rather than a health concern.
copy.fact: Silverfish are older than dinosaurs — they were doing this exact job 100 million years before T. rex.
copy.blurb: Mostly a storage-box nuisance. Lots of them signals a humidity problem worth fixing.

tech_notes: Moisture-driven; check garage/attic/closet humidity. Covered under general pest program; dehumidifying helps long-term.

traits: Rear pincers (harmless to people), 12-16 mm, dark brown
Hides under pots, mats, and mulch during the day
Voracious predator of caterpillars, aphids, and other small insects

look_alikes.difference: Earwigs have rear pincers and a beetle-like body; silverfish have three tail bristles instead of pincers and a tapered, scaly body.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the tail end — pincers versus bristles.

copy.what_it_means: The pincers look dramatic but are harmless to people — they’re for folding wings and courtship, not attacking. Earwigs are voracious predators of other garden insects; fixing door sweeps and drainage usually stops indoor wandering.
copy.fact: The pincers are for folding its wings and courtship — the ear-crawling myth is pure medieval legend.
copy.blurb: Fix door sweeps and drainage; the visitors stop themselves.

tech_notes: Minor nuisance; beneficial predator of caterpillars/aphids likely outweighs plant nibbling. Exterior perimeter + exclusion advice covers it.
